newsitem.title: UK: New UK underwriting approach seen posing some risk.
newsitem.headline: New UK underwriting approach seen posing some risk.

text.p: A more flexible approach to the fee structure for underwriting share issues in Britain should strike a balance between revolutionising the current system and guaranteeing access to capital, industry representatives said on Friday.
But they warned against a swing too far away from the present system, saying there was a risk some companies could find themselves charged more than before for access to capital.

In an innovative deal on Thursday for underwriting a 220 million stg rights issue for Scottish-based hotel and casinos group Stakis Plc merchant banking group Schroders put one third of the sub-underwriting out to tender.
Competitive bidding at lower rates of commission saved Stakis 400,000 stg or over eight percent of what it would have paid if the fees had been fixed as they usually are.

But how eager institutions are to underwrite a particular issue could depend on factors including, for example, the number of shares offered, appetite in the stock market for new issues, and on how the company raising the capital is perceived.

"The balance you've got to maintain is revolutionising the whole thing and maintaining a system that has worked," said Richard Regan, head of investments at the Association of British Insurers, the body representing many of the big investment funds which guarantee to take a proportion of the shares in an issue.
"It is a system which allows companies to be guaranteed they will be getting cash, so let's not destroy that system which gives this guarantee," Regan told Reuters.

The tender was in part a response to pressure from Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT), which is likely early next year to decide whether to refer the practice for study by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC), and could be followed by other similarly underwritten share issues before this year is out.

Thursday's move by Schroders was the first innovation for decades in the underwriting structure of the London equity market. Until yesterday, all companies paid a commission of roughly two percent to those assisting in a rights issue. For sub-underwriting, the fee is usually 1.25 percent.

The ABI was one of three industry bodies which in September urged members towards greater flexibility over underwriting charges, heading off what could have been an earlier decision by the OFT on referral to the MMC and the publication of an OFT report on the fixed underwriting fee structure.

But it remains unclear whether ABI's efforts, those of Schroders and any other merchant bank which decides to follow, will prevent a referral to the MMC. While regarding this tender as a positive step, the regulator wants further progress.

The OFT's director general John Bridgeman is, meantime, considering whether to publish results from a survey of nearly 100 companies who made rights issues over the 12 months to the end of May this year. The findings from this survey were not expected to show much evidence of flexibility on fees. While not in itself the key decision from the regulator everyone is waiting for -- whether the report appears or not and how much is published if it is released will be one indication to what extent Bridgeman feels the situation has moved on.
